claim: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) modelled scientific reasoning as search in two spaces, hypotheses and experiments (SDDS).
authors: Klahr D, Dunbar K
title: Dual Space Search During Scientific Reasoning
transfer: Schema keeps two separate loops: propose hypothesis, then design an experiment that discriminates. Do not mix the two in one call.

claim: In the Klahr-Dunbar study, participants who could not produce the right rule from memory sometimes found it only by generalizing from experiment results; two hypothesis-generation strategies were memory search and generalizing from results.
authors: Klahr D, Dunbar K
title: Dual Space Search During Scientific Reasoning
transfer: When recall of a known rule fails, switch to experiment-driven induction (run probes, then generalize) rather than re-sampling hypotheses.

claim: Schunn and Klahr (1995) extended SDDS to a 4-space model that adds spaces for data representation and experimental paradigm.
authors: Schunn CD, Klahr D
title: A 4-Space Model of Scientific Discovery
venue: Proceedings of the Cognitive Science Society
transfer: Add an explicit representation-change step (how to encode the data) as a third search space beside hypothesis and test.

claim: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider and Rhenius (1999) used matchstick arithmetic to show that impasses break through constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition, and that problem difficulty followed predictions from the amount of constraint relaxation or chunk decomposition needed.
authors: Knoblich G, Ohlsson S, Haider H, Rhenius D
title: Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
n: four experiments (n per experiment not read; PDF was an unreadable scan)
transfer: On stuck items, force a re-encoding: loosen one assumed constraint, or split a familiar chunk into parts, then retry. Trigger only after a failed attempt.

claim: Oellinger, Jones and Knoblich (2006) found a strong effect of representational change on solution rates and only a minimal effect of heuristics.
authors: Oellinger M, Jones G, Knoblich G
title: Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks
transfer: On insight-type items, spend calls on changing the representation rather than on deeper search with the same encoding.

claim: A later review judged the evidence that insight is a sudden restructuring (central to representational change theory) to be inconclusive.
authors: review cited via search summary (MDPI J. Intelligence 11(5):86)
title: insight problem solving review (title not confirmed)
transfer: Do not build the schema on a claim that insight is a distinct sudden mechanism; treat re-encoding as one useful move among others.

claim: Reasoners who give a biased intuitive answer still show lower confidence on conflict problems than on no-conflict controls, about 10 percentage points lower, in base-rate (N=247) and conjunction (N=147) tasks.
quote: acknowledge that their intuitive answers are not fully warranted
authors: De Neys W, Cromheeke S, Osman M
title: Biased but in doubt: conflict and decision confidence
transfer: Use a cheap conflict signal: ask the model for a quick intuitive answer and a rival heuristic answer; if they differ, route to checking. Agreement means skip. Effect sizes: eta2p .18 and .14.

claim: On conflict problems the intuitive-biased answer was correct only about 20% (base rate) and 24% (conjunction) of the time in undergraduates, so the first answer is usually wrong on designed trap items.
authors: De Neys W, Cromheeke S, Osman M
title: Biased but in doubt: conflict and decision confidence
transfer: Our puzzles are not trap items (first answer right 56-92%); the router must tell trap-style tasks from ordinary ones, so do not generalize the low base rate.

claim: De Neys (2012) argues that reasoners have intuitive sensitivity to logical principles, detect conflict with a biased answer, and often fail to override it; this is the 'logical intuitions' view.
authors: De Neys W
title: Bias and conflict: A case for logical intuitions
transfer: The main failure is not detection but override: when a conflict is flagged, require a concrete test that decides, not another opinion.

claim: Bago and De Neys (2017), using a two-response paradigm with time pressure and memory load, found correct logical answers are often given as the first, immediate response; a BPS summary reports about 30% logical at once, about 10% corrected by deliberation, about half wrong and kept.
authors: Bago B, De Neys W
title: Fast logic? Examining the time course assumption of dual process theory
n: four experiments, 'hundreds of participants' per summary
transfer: Matches our data: deliberation fixed few answers (~10%) and first answers were often already right. Log first answer and final answer separately to count flips each way. Percentages come from a summary, not the paper.

claim: Lower confidence in the first answer predicted more reflection and more answer changes in Bago and De Neys.
authors: Bago B, De Neys W (as reported by BPS Research Digest)
title: Fast logic? Examining the time course assumption of dual process theory
transfer: Gate extra deliberation on low first-answer confidence or probe disagreement, not on a fixed rule.

claim: Thompson, Prowse Turner and Pennycook (2011) proposed that a feeling of rightness attached to the intuitive answer sets the probability of switching to analytic thinking; later work ties it to answer fluency.
authors: Thompson VA, Prowse Turner JA, Pennycook G
title: Intuition, reason, and metacognition
transfer: Machine feeling of rightness: agreement across quick samples and speed of convergence. Original not opened; claim known via citing papers.

claim: Pennycook, Fugelsang and Koehler (2015) say conflict detection and decoupling are dissociable sources of analytic thought and conflict detection sometimes fails.
quote: conflict detection and decoupling are dissociable sources of Type 2 processing and 2) conflict detection sometimes fails
authors: Pennycook G, Fugelsang JA, Koehler DJ
title: What makes us think? A three-stage dual-process model of analytic engagement
transfer: Make conflict detection (do two cues disagree?) and override (run a decisive test) two separate schema steps, each logged.

claim: The Alter et al. (2007) finding that hard-to-read fonts raise Cognitive Reflection Test scores did not replicate: pooling the original with 16 replications gave no effect on solution rates.
quote: we find no effect on solution rates
authors: Meyer A, Frederick S, Burnham TC, et al.
title: Disfluent fonts don't help people solve math problems
transfer: Warning: cheap cues meant to trigger 'slow thinking' do not reliably work. For the agent, a prompt-level nudge to 'think carefully' should be measured, not assumed.

claim: Unconscious thought advantage: a large replication found no effect (Hedges g = -0.01, N=399); a meta-analysis of 61 effect sizes gave g = 0.15 that fell to 0.018 after trim-and-fill, so no reliable advantage of distraction over deliberation.
quote: Consistent with the reliability account, the large-scale replication study yielded no evidence for the UTA
authors: Nieuwenstein MR, Wierenga T, Morey RD, et al.
title: On making the right choice: A meta-analysis and large-scale replication attempt of the unconscious thought advantage
transfer: No support for an 'incubation by distraction' call gap in the schema for choice tasks; spend those calls on explicit evaluation instead.

claim: Stanovich and West (2008) report across seven studies that many thinking biases (conjunction, framing, anchoring, base-rate neglect, myside, sunk cost) are uncorrelated with cognitive ability; belief bias, denominator neglect, probability matching and 4-card matching bias do correlate.
authors: Stanovich KE, West RF
title: On the relative independence of thinking biases and cognitive ability
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 94:672-695
transfer: A stronger model will not remove myside and anchoring biases by itself; the schema needs structural debiasing (consider-the-opposite, independent evidence) for these. Known via a blog summary only.

claim: Stanovich, West and Toplak's review reports that myside bias magnitude shows very little relation to intelligence, and that avoiding it is a rational thinking skill that intelligence tests do not capture.
authors: Stanovich KE, West RF, Toplak ME
title: Myside bias, rational thinking, and intelligence
n: over 1,400 students in two experiments, per search summary
transfer: Generate the case for the other side as a separate call with the opposite position assigned, since self-reflection will not correct it.

claim: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2017) argue mental models usually represent only what is true, which saves memory but makes people commit systematic fallacies in inferences that need false cases.
authors: Khemlani S, Johnson-Laird PN
title: Illusions in Reasoning
transfer: For logic items, enumerate possibilities explicitly, including the false cases of each clause, before concluding.

claim: mReasoner, an implementation of mental model theory, has a parameter for how often a reasoner reconsiders a conclusion and searches for counterexamples (SYSTM2), and it was fitted to humans and language models on syllogisms.
authors: Bertolazzi et al. (arXiv, author list not confirmed)
title: A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
transfer: Counterexample search is a tunable amount, not a switch; test 0, 1 and 2 passes. Results of the fit were not read.

claim: Newell and Simon (1972) framed problem solving as search through a problem space, with means-ends analysis and subgoals as key heuristics, studied with think-aloud protocols and Tower of Hanoi and river-crossing tasks.
authors: Newell A, Simon HA
title: Human Problem Solving
transfer: Make the state, operators and goal test explicit in the schema; use subgoal decomposition when the goal gap is large. Book not opened.

claim: Kotovsky, Hayes and Simon (1985) studied why isomorphic Tower of Hanoi problems differ in difficulty; Kotovsky and Simon (1990) extended this to problem-space difficulty. Findings not read.
authors: Kotovsky K, Hayes JR, Simon HA
title: Why are some problems hard? Evidence from Tower of Hanoi
transfer: Surface rewording of the same problem can change difficulty; run one reworded restatement as a cheap diversity source.

claim: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski report that early GPT models made human-like intuitive errors on cognitive reflection tests, which mostly disappeared in ChatGPT models.
authors: Hagendorff T, Fabi S, Kosinski M
title: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in large language models but disappeared in ChatGPT
transfer: Trap-style items that fool humans may not fool current models; test the router on trap items before assuming forced doubt is needed. Carried from the earlier brief, not re-opened.
